topic: Opening: civilisation as an argument

Whether it is the earliest use is contested: the Collège de France reports that recent lexicographic tools find the word earlier, and in English before French

topic: Case C: chintz and the Calico Acts
claim: The Calico Act of 1721 (7 Geo. I c. 7), in force from 25 December 1722, banned wearing or using printed, painted, stained or dyed calicoes, to protect wool and silk; the 1736 Act recites its exceptions as "Muslins, Neckcloths and Fustians". The 1736 Act (9 Geo. II c. 4) then allowed British-printed cloth with an all-linen warp and cotton weft, and printers worked those fustians for the home market. Whether calicoes dyed all blue were also excepted is not confirmed in the text read.

topic: Generative AI; unit framing
claim: Training generative AI on makers' work: reading 1, some training uses may be transformative, and a UK court held (4 November 2025) that model weights which store no images are not an "infringing copy". Reading 2, commercial use of "vast troves" of works to make competing content, "especially where... illegal access", goes beyond fair use (US Copyright Office, May 2025). The unit does not rule. Status, as of the latest dated sources (July–August 2026): the UK ruling is under appeal. On 16 December 2025 the trial judge gave Getty permission to appeal the "infringing copy" point, as a novel point of law; she refused Stability permission on the trade mark findings, and Stability asked the Court of Appeal directly. No Court of Appeal hearing or judgment was found; commentators expected a hearing in late 2026 at the earliest. Getty's separate US case continues. The Copyright Office report is still the May 2025 pre-publication version. Unit framing: copying is a normal engine of making; it becomes a wrong through a false mark, a taken market or no transformation. This framing is interpretive.
confidence_note: contested — both readings; framing interpretive; status documented as of the dates given

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Shen Xinyu and Li Yu printed the *Mustard Seed Garden Manual* in 1679; Wang Gai illustrated it by adapting an earlier primer. It gave painters without a collection "a glimpse into the elite training available to painters of privilege". Reprinted in colour in Japan in 1748; Japanese artists "copied actual compositions from it".

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Calligraphy practice pages (siyah mashq) were "intended to strengthen a calligrapher's hand and instill discipline through the repetition of letters"; after the 16th century they became an art form in their own right.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Ruskin (1853): "It is not, truly speaking, the labor that is divided; but the men" (chapter VI, §XVI, as Gutenberg 30755 spells it).

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The Government School of Design opened in 1837 at Somerset House, after a Commons committee of 1835. It taught the figure "as applied to Ornament" for manufactures; a separate female school is listed in 1848. In 1865 the J.J. School in Bombay (founded 1857) hired Lockwood Kipling and John Griffiths from South Kensington.
source: https://www.rca.ac.uk/more/history/ ; https://sculpture.gla.ac.uk/mapping/public/view/organization.php?id=msib4_1267714397 ; https://dagworld.com/the-school-and-the-city-the-j-j-school-of-art-in-bombay.html [depth: Summary; database entry; gallery article (2024)]

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The Met's vase was made "by the Bombay School of Art in an effort to preserve Indian craft", with motifs from the Ajanta murals and a shape showing "British neoclassical taste". It "may have been produced" for the London Colonial and Indian Exhibition of 1886.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The Mayo School of Industrial Art opened in Lahore in 1875 with Kipling as first principal, "to document the arts and crafts of the Punjab" and train craftsmen for "craft production". It became the National College of Arts in 1956–58.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Two readings of the colonial school. Preservation: the Met and NCA describe schools set up to preserve and document craft. Division: a 2025 essay argues the system "divided mind from hand, theory from skill".
source: Met 839471; NCA (claim 8); https://thefridaytimes.com/06-Nov-2025/nca-150-colonial-legacies-artistic-identity-future-art-education [depth: Label; institutional page; opinion essay]

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Ram Singh trained as a carpenter, became Vice-Principal of the Mayo School, and was commissioned "to design the decoration" of the Durbar Room (RCT). English Heritage's Google Arts & Culture story says the room "was designed by John Lockwood Kipling", with moulds made under Ram Singh's supervision; English Heritage's own Osborne page says it was "Designed by … Lockwood Kipling, and master carver Bhai Ram Singh".
confidence_note: Contested (credit; English Heritage gives both wordings, fact-check 3 Oct 2026)

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919; it moved to Dessau in 1925 and Berlin in 1932; its dissolution was announced on 10 August 1933. Each workshop had a Werkmeister for craft and a Formmeister for form. Klee taught from May 1921 and led the bookbinding, metal and stained-glass workshops.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Gropius's manifesto (April 1919): "Architekten, Bildhauer, Maler, wir alle müssen zum Handwerk zurück!" Quote by jurisdiction: one short line, in German with our own gloss, linked to the source; the text is in EU copyright to the end of 2039 (TXT032).

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The 1919 programme admitted students regardless of age and sex; in summer 1919, 84 women and 79 men enrolled. Gropius soon asked for sharp selection of women, who were steered into weaving. Link F1.18.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Lenin's government founded Vkhutemas, by decree of 29 November 1920 (Getty ULAN), as "a merger of a fine arts college and a crafts school". It offered free education, admitted students "regardless of their artistic talent or academic standing", and had five production departments. It was restructured as Vkhutein in 1926–28.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Inge Scholl, Otl Aicher and Max Bill founded the HfG Ulm in 1953; it taught from 1955 to 1968 and was a model for schools in India and Brazil. ESDI in Rio was created by decree 1.443 of 25 December 1962 on the HfG Ulm model.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The Government of India asked the Ford Foundation to invite Charles and Ray Eames; their India Report is dated 7 April 1958. NID was established in 1961, as the National Institute of Industrial Design; Gira and Gautam Sarabhai were central to it, with "learning by doing".

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: Kala Bhavana was founded at Santiniketan in 1919; Nandalal Bose became principal in 1923. Its teachers took up "Santhal studies", nature study and local landscape.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The Egyptian School of Fine Arts opened on 13 May 1908 (REM; the Fine Arts faculty's own history gives 12 May), with drawing at its core. Prince Youssef Kamal paid for it; it was free, came under the Ministry of Education in 1910, and trained Mahmoud Mokhtar.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The Kumasi art school began as an art department at Achimota between the wars, after a "Hand and Eye Work" curriculum introduced around 1909. It moved to the Kumasi College of Technology (1952), which became KNUST in 1961.

topic: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
claim: The Academy of San Carlos in Mexico City, led by the engraver Jerónimo Antonio Gil, is "the earliest art academy in the Americas"; students drew from plaster casts. Its three dates are three acts: a provisional school from 1781, a royal cédula in 1783, and the inauguration of classes on 4 November 1785.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: The unit's framing: modernism was many movements made in many centres, each choosing a past and a refusal; this can be taught without ranking them.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Pevsner's *Pioneers of the Modern Movement from William Morris to Walter Gropius* (London: Faber, 1936) called Morris "the father of the Modern Movement" and closed: "So our circle is complete." MoMA's 1949 edition retitled it *Pioneers of Modern Design*.
source: https://archive.org/details/pioneersofmodern0000pevs_s8e4 ; http://problemata.org/en/articles/605 (Sunwoo, *Getty Research Journal* 2, 2010) [depth: Catalogue record; article]

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: UNESCO (2016) says the Capitol Complex at Chandigarh "symbolized India's accession to modernity" and that Le Corbusier's influence reached "four continents".

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Stalin, 18 May 1925: "Proletarian in content, national in form—such is the universal culture towards which socialism is proceeding."

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: On 23 April 1932 the Central Committee liquidated the proletarian writers' associations and ordered "an analogous change in policy for other forms of art".

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Tashkent's Navoi Theatre, by Alexey Shchusev, opened in 1947. Soviet Koreans worked on it from 1943; Japanese prisoners of war "assisted" in the final phase.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Uzbekistan's heritage list names Usto Shirin Muradov as a leading ganch carver of the Navoi Theatre's decoration.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Resolution No. 1871 of 4 November 1955 condemned "errors" in architecture and required "the most economical standard designs" and industrial methods.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: The earthquake of 26 April 1966 led to Tashkent's rebuilding; ten buildings of the 1960s to early 1990s were inscribed by UNESCO in 2026 for adapting "standardised systems to regional materials, traditions".

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: The Peoples' Friendship Palace (1981; Yevgeny Rozanov, Elena Sukhanova) has a façade of "panjara screens reimagined in concrete and stone"; the former Lenin Museum's prefabricated panels "echo Islamic motifs".

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: On 25 March 2024 Uzbekistan's government listed about 157 mosaic panels as monumental art. Not all mosaics are covered; a panel by Arnold Gan was dismantled in September 2023.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: In Almaty "dozens of works of monumental art were produced at the Oner Art Combine by brigades of craftsmen". The mosaic *Qyz Zhibek* (1971, Wedding Palace) is by Nikolai Tsivchinsky and Moldakhmet Kenbaev. Landmark protection is weak.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded at Belgrade, 1–6 September 1961; founders included Ghana, India, Morocco, Cuba and Yugoslavia. MoMA calls Yugoslav architecture "both in line with and distinct from" design elsewhere.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Two readings of tropical modernism. Fry and Drew built for "comfort, mainly to British administrators" against anti-colonial struggle. Nkrumah "reappropriated" it as a symbol; Owusu-Addo returned to teach at KNUST.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Nehru recruited Fry and Drew in 1950 for Chandigarh. The Met's label credits the furniture to Pierre Jeanneret; The Conversation names Eulie Chowdhury as co-designer of a chair. Siegel's *Provenance* traces the pieces from offices to auction.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Senegal set up a national tapestry works at Thiès in 1966; opening it on 4 December 1966, Senghor called for "un art nouveau pour une nation nouvelle". Four weavers trained in France: Mamadou Wade, Mar Fall, Doudou Diagne, Alioune Badara Diakhaté.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Brasília was built 1956–1960 to plans by Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer, under Kubitschek; UNESCO inscribed it in 1987.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Yanagi, Kawai Kanjirō and Hamada Shōji coined "mingei" in 1925; the Japan Folk Crafts Museum opened in 1936. Yanagi remounted Met 1975.268.147; Hamada made its knobs.

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Two readings of Mingei. Brandt: "shaped by imperialism and colonialism". Kikuchi: Yanagi defended the Gwanghwamun gate (1922) and opened a Korean folk art museum in Seoul (1924), yet did not question colonial rule. Ch'oe Harim (1974) called it "aesthetics of colonialism".
source: https://www.dukeupress.edu/kingdom-of-beauty ; https://ualresearchonline.arts.ac.uk/id/eprint/11777/1/Kikuchi-Yanagi%20Soetsu%20and%20Korean%20crafts%20within%20the%20Mingei%20movement.pdf (Yuko Kikuchi, *BAKS* 5, 1994, pp. 23–38) [depth: Publisher summary; full text (article, 1994)]

topic: Modernisms, plural
claim: Three reach-backs. Zaria's Natural Synthesis (late 1950s) drew on uli, an Igbo women's painting practice; Okeke learned it from his mother. Tate places the Casablanca School in the "rebirth that followed Morocco's independence". Antropofagia (1928) proposed a "symbolic digestion of external influences" (MoMA).

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Mitsui Takatoshi opened the Echigoya drapery in Edo in 1673. In 1683 it moved to Surugachō and sold for cash at fixed prices (*genkin kakene nashi*). Kiyonaga (about 1789) and Hokusai (about 1830–32) printed the shop.
source: https://www.imhds.co.jp/corporate/business/department/history/history-mitsukoshi.html (company history) ; https://mitsui-bunko.or.jp/archives/eng_story04/ ; https://the-shashi.com/en/tse/8231/ ; records in section 5 [depth: company history; summaries; full records]

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Mitsukoshi Gofukuten was incorporated in 1904 and issued a "Department Store Declaration" the same month, after display selling (1895) and the end of seated selling (1900).

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Paul and Justin Videau founded Au Bon Marché in Paris in 1838. Aristide Boucicaut joined in 1852 and brought in fixed prices, exchanges and refunds. Staff reached 1,888 by 1879. Marguerite Boucicaut ran it after his death.
confidence_note: documented (1,888 staff and Marguerite's role still from Wikipedia)

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Which store was the earliest department store is contested. **Reading A:** Le Bon Marché after 1852 was "one of the first modern department stores". **Reading B:** cash selling at fixed prices ran at the Echigoya from 1683; the Mitsui archive says there were "no examples even in foreign countries". The unit asks what "department store" is taken to mean.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Worth worked at Gagelin, then opened his own firm with a partner in 1858; his designs were shown on live models.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Worth sewed his name into his garments, often called the earliest designer label. By the late 1880s the house held twice-yearly collections; staff grew from about 50 to over 1,200.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: The Paris trade body was founded in 1868 and became the Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne on 14 December 1910. "Haute Couture" became a legally registered designation on 23 January 1945.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: "Uncle Josh Weathersby in a department store" (label variant "Uncle Josh in a department store"), written and spoken by Cal Stewart, recorded 22 May 1903 (Philadelphia, place unconfirmed), 10-in. Victor 665, pre-matrix B-665, take M-7. The same number also covers 7-in. takes of 1901 and 1903 and an 8-in. remake of 1906, so cite matrix and take. US recordings published before 1923 entered the public domain on 1 January 2022.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: In the printed monologue, Josh asks for muslin and calico, is insulted by a floor worker, and chases his change through the cash carrier.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Kalighat pictures were sold as pilgrimage and tourist souvenirs from at least the 1830s to the 1930s, made "cheaply, quickly, and in vast numbers". A master pencilled the form; family members inked it. Buyers included villagers, Marwari merchants, English officials and missionaries.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Words on kanga began in the early 1900s, in Swahili in Arabic script, later in Roman letters. The practice is credited to Kaderdina Hajee "Abdulla" Essak of Mombasa, at his wife's suggestion. Where the earliest machine-printed kanga was made (Germany, England or India) is uncertain.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: A Linotype went into commercial use at the *New York Tribune* in July 1886 (first used on 3 July), the earliest known installation. It cast whole lines from molten metal. Photo and digital setting largely replaced it in the 1970s–80s.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: In 1954 Kamel Mrowa, founder of *Al-Hayat* in Beirut, approached Linotype & Machinery Ltd. Simplified Arabic cut the character count so Arabic fitted one 90-channel magazine. Compugraphic later copied it.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: China set up the "748 Project" in August 1974. Wang Xuan stored characters as outlines and parametric strokes; Chen Kunqiu designed and built the large-scale software. A book printed in 1980 marked the move from "lead and fire" to "light and electricity"; the *Economic Daily* dropped lead type in 1988.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Fiona Ross and Tim Holloway designed Linotype Bengali, 1978–82, for newspaper composition. Ross says early fonts were "hampered by hot-metal technology".

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Unicode 1.0.0 appeared in October 1991, 1.0.1 in June 1992, 18.0.0 on 16 September 2026. Han unification gives Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese Han characters shared code points, decided by experts from those countries. **Reading A:** one code per shared character; fonts show local forms. **Reading B:** critics, especially in Japan, say forms that matter were merged and plain text loses them.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: In October 2013 Etsy let sellers hire staff, outsource shipping and use manufacturers, if they showed "authorship of the idea" and "transparency on who and what is helping create the item". Solo sellers protested.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: A "Taobao village" has at least 100 active online shops and 10 million yuan of yearly sales. There were 20 in 2013 and 4,310 in 2019. Furniture sellers in Dongfeng village, Jiangsu, drove a delivery trade.

topic: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
claim: Training models on makers' work. **Reading 1:** highly transformative uses weigh toward fair use; a UK court held (4 November 2025) that model weights are not an "infringing copy". **Reading 2:** training to make competing expressive content is "less likely to be deemed fair", and pirated sources weigh against it (US Copyright Office, May 2025, pre-publication). The UK court did not decide training, which happened abroad; Getty was granted permission to appeal in January 2026. **Unit framing:** each new counter (shop, label, type machine, standard, platform) resets the terms between maker and buyer, and the consumer was made in many places. This framing is interpretive.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: The unit's framing: extraction is measured by stock, labour, distance and waste, and substitution moves weight rather than removing it.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Congo (Kinshasa) mined 226,000 of the world's 302,000 tonnes of cobalt in 2024, "an estimated 73% of world total"; in 2025 it temporarily banned cobalt exports.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Amnesty and Afrewatch (January 2016) cited a UNICEF estimate that in 2014 about 40,000 children worked in all the mines across southern Congo, many in cobalt; some were aged seven. Later counts measure different things: the US Department of Labor (*2022 Findings*) gives 5,000–35,000 children in artisanal cobalt mining and says the exact number is unknown; the ILO (20 November 2024) reported over 6,200 children registered in mining in Haut-Katanga and Lualaba. Amnesty traced cobalt from artisanal miners through traders to Congo Dongfang Mining (Huayou Cobalt), then to battery-component makers.
confidence_note: Documented (each figure as its source dates and defines it; none is a census)
source: https://www.amnesty.org/en/srv/htdocs/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/AFR6231832016ENGLISH.pdf (AFR 62/3183/2016) ; https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2098480.html (USDOL) ; https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/ilo-launches-galab-project-democratic-republic-congo-address-child-labour (ILO) [depth: Full report; government report; press release]

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Under Leopold II (1885–1908), rubber and ivory exploitation "was accompanied by excessive violence". The death toll is uncertain: the museum gives a population deficit of "hundreds of thousands" and says recent estimates "may even be several million". Give both.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: A sentry told Casement he was holding eleven women "to compel their husbands to bring in the right amount of rubber".

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Two readings of how red rubber ended. Reform: English and Belgian campaigners. Depletion: in the Abir concession the system had broken down by 1906 because the rubber was exhausted, before the European debate took hold (Harms).

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Peru exported guano commercially from 1840, mainly from the Chincha Islands. It was dug and loaded by enslaved people, later by local Indigenous workers (the source's "local Indians"), convicts and thousands of indentured workers, mostly from south China.
source: https://heritage.lrfoundation.org.uk/stories/guano-the-perilous-cargo-of-flammable-and-noxious-fertiliser (R. and L. Adkins, undated) [depth: Full text (article)]

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Between 1849 and 1874 nearly 100,000 Chinese men were brought to Peru, many "kidnapped or lured". They worked guano fields, railways and plantations, 14 to 16 hours a day. New arrivals ended in 1874.
source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/chinese-labor-peru (Peloso, *Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture*) [depth: Summary (encyclopedia entry)]

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Humberstone and Santa Laura processed "the largest deposit of saltpeter in the world" from 1880. Over 200 works stood in the region; workers came from Chile, Peru and Bolivia; the product was sodium nitrate fertiliser. Inscribed 2005; in Danger 2005–2019.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: In the 16th century Potosí was "regarded as the world's largest industrial complex". Its mita was "mandatory labour"; UNESCO gives about 13,500 Indigenous workers forced into the mines by the 17th century. In Danger since 2014.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Bengal's indigo revolt ran from March 1859 into 1860. Planters had tied ryots by advances and contracts to grow indigo on their best land, often into debt. The commission's August 1860 report said ryots could not be forced; Dinabandhu Mitra's play *Nil Darpan* (1860) spread the case.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Synthetic indigo was launched in 1897 by BASF and Hoechst; planters and the colonial state funded science to compete. BASF says the synthesis took 17 years and 18 million gold marks.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: "In the 1880s American-type cotton was introduced" in Russian Central Asia.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Cleveland 2016.89 is silk embroidery on six strips of plain-weave cotton, 1800–1850, "probably embroidered in Shakhrisyabz". The museum says such textiles "were essential items in dowries" and dates the type after "sericulture was introduced in the Merv area around 1800".
confidence_note: Probable (place and date, as the museum hedges them)

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: In the 1960s the Soviet Union diverted the Aral Sea's two rivers for cotton and other crops. The sea had been the world's fourth largest lake; by 2014 the South Aral's eastern lobe was gone. Fisheries collapsed; chemical-laden dust became a health hazard.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: In 1960 the Aral Sea covered about 66,000–67,500 km² and held about 1,060 km³. By 2014 it covered about 10% of that area and held under 10% of that volume. River inflow fell from 47–55 to 3–20 km³ a year. A 2025 remote-sensing review puts the remaining water at about 5,250 km², about 8% of the original area.
source: https://wmo.int/media/magazine-article/future-of-aral-sea-lies-transboundary-co-operation (Harriman, WMO Bulletin, 1 March 2014) ; https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/17/16/2814 (*Remote Sensing* 17(16), 2025) [depth: Full text (articles)]

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: The ILO found Uzbekistan's 2021 cotton harvest free of systemic child and forced labour, from about 11,000 interviews; about 1% of pickers reported coercion.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: China mined 270,000 of about 380,000 tonnes of rare earths in 2024 (USGS, February 2026). In 2012 NASA said about half of China's output came from Bayan Obo, with acid waste gas, wastewater and radioactive residue from processing.

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: In 1556 Agricola recorded critics who said mining fells woods and groves, kills beasts and birds, and "poisons the brooks and streams". He set their case out to answer it.
source: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/38015/pg38015.txt (*De re metallica*, Book I, Hoover translation, 1912) [depth: Full text]

topic: The planetary present: making as extraction
claim: Levi Strauss & Co. estimated one pair of 501 jeans at 3,781 litres of water and 33.4 kg CO2e over its life. Fibre is 68% of the water; consumer care is 37% of the climate impact. Based on the 2012 production year.

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: The unit's framing: an object's use-life belongs to its design history; wear, repair, resale and inheritance are evidence.
source: Our own argument (Kopytoff, 1986, not opened) [depth: n/a]

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Met 16.122.5 is a 13th-century Longquan tea bowl with gold lacquer repairs. Chinese celadons were "highly valued in Japan since the fourteenth century"; in China broken ceramics "were typically mended with metal staples".

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: The bowl was used in Japan. The Met infers it: "Because kintsugi is a technique unique to Japan, its presence … suggests that the object was once used and cherished there." No owner or repair date is recorded.

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Cleveland 1918.454, a Goryeo bottle of the 1200s–1300s, has a lip "repaired with gold lacquer". The record holds both readings. Reading A: its description says the technique was "Initiated in 15th-century Japan" and that Goryeo celadons were treasures "among modern collectors", so the repair is later. Reading B: its "did you know" note says the method "was extensively used for ceramic works in the Goryeo period, such as this one". The record dates neither repair.
confidence_note: Contested (both readings, both in the record)

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: The Bakōhan (Tokyo National Museum, TG-2354, Important Cultural Property) is Longquan ware of the Southern Song, 13th century. Itō Tōgai's record of 1727 says it was given to Taira no Shigemori about 1175, and that Ashikaga Yoshimasa later sent it cracked to China for a replacement; it returned clamped. The museum judges the Shigemori story unlikely on the bowl's style and the Yoshimasa episode credible.
confidence_note: Documented (object, record); probable (the Yoshimasa episode, as the holder judges it)

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Ger making (UNESCO, 2013) is household work, "with men carving the wood and both women and men engaged in painting, sewing and stitching, and felt-making". Mongol nomad migration (UNESCO, 2024): children learn "assembling and disassembling yurts".

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Mongolian felt is made in late summer or early autumn by families together; a sheet of old felt, *ekh esgii* ("mother felt"), is the model for the new.
source: https://ncch.gov.mn/ich?ItemID=14 (National Center for Cultural Heritage) [depth: Summary (register page)]

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Met 22.100.42, an ensi, "likely served … to cover the entrance to a Turkmen tent"; seasonal migration required that "every possession—even their homes—be collapsible and portable". Chuvals (Met 22.100.40a) held family belongings, "akin to a wardrobe".

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Kyrgyz ala-kiyiz and shyrdak (Urgent Safeguarding List, 2012) warmed and decorated nomads' homes; skills pass from older to younger women within the family.

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Cleveland 1921.556 (c. 1875–80, "woman artist") mixes handspun, Germantown and bayeta wool; "wearing blankets, which were worn around the shoulders, were purchased as rugs".

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Cleveland 1937.903 (c. 1900) is a rug modelled on the "chief blanket", though the Diné had no chiefs; after Bosque Redondo weavers turned to goods for outside collectors.

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: The US Army "slaughtered sheep by the thousands"; more than 8,000 Diné walked over 300 miles to Bosque Redondo, were held four years, and returned in 1868.

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: After the 1894 wool-tariff removal, in the 1890s "the Navajo blanket was transformed into a rug and weavers' productivity quadrupled"; traders bought textiles "by weight until the 1960s".

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
claim: Kanthas were made by women for their own homes from "old, worn sari lengths" (V&A). Small kanthas "are used to wrap babies"; kanthas "form part of the dowry of brides in certain parts of Bangladesh and West Bengal" (Zaman and Stevulak).

topic: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy
claim: Mercury gilding came into general use in China around the Warring States period. It became common in Han noble tombs. Its makers knew mercury vapour was harmful. Whether this buckle was mercury-gilded is untested.

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy
claim: The Met says its Xianbei plaque pair "once adorned a leather belt belonging to a member of a nomadic community, likely the Xianbei, that migrated seasonally".

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy
claim: Bayeta is trade cloth, ravelled and reused as weft. Germantown is commercial American yarn dyed with aniline, first made in Germantown, Pennsylvania. Aniline dyes were first made commercially in 1856. Churro sheep came with the Spanish in 1598.

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy

topic: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
claim: CARE was written for "Indigenous data". Applying its four questions to non-Indigenous source communities (the Kolhapuri makers) is our extension, labelled as such. We borrow CARE's questions, not its authority: we never call a non-Indigenous community's protocol "CARE" or present it as Indigenous data governance, which is what GIDA says CARE is for (https://www.gida-global.org/care).

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
claim: CARE (RDA International Indigenous Data Sovereignty Interest Group, September 2019). Authority to Control: "Indigenous Peoples' rights and interests in Indigenous data must be recognised and their authority to control such data be empowered". A3: the right "to develop cultural governance protocols". E3: future use and harm.
source: Same PDF; Carroll et al., *Data Science Journal* 19 (2020), art. 43, CC BY 4.0: https://datascience.codata.org/articles/10.5334/dsj-2020-043

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
claim: Local Contexts: "Labels are for use by Indigenous communities"; Notices are for institutions and researchers; both are "extra-legal mechanisms". Icons "may not be altered"; icons and template texts © Local Contexts, all rights reserved.

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
claim: Fees: "Local Contexts and the Hub will always be free for Indigenous communities." Institutions and researchers subscribe: Individual free; Collections Care Notices free for institutions; Small US$1,250, Medium US$5,000, Large US$10,000 a year. "As of 2025, a subscription is required" to use Notices.

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
claim: UNDRIP (A/RES/61/295, 13 Sept 2007; 143 for, 4 against, 11 abstaining). Art. 11.2: redress for cultural property "taken without their free, prior and informed consent". Art. 19: consult "through their own representative institutions".

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
claim: UNESCO adopted the 2003 Convention on 17 October 2003 in Paris; it entered into force on 20 April 2006 (https://ich.unesco.org/en/states-parties-00024). Art. 2.1 defines intangible heritage as what "communities, groups and, in some cases, individuals recognize as part of their cultural heritage"; Art. 2.2 lists "traditional craftsmanship"; Art. 15 asks for "the widest possible participation" of communities.

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
claim: UNESCO's Ethical Principles (decision 10.COM 15.a, Windhoek, 2015): principle 4, "free, prior, sustained and informed consent"; principle 5, customary access practices respected "even where these may limit broader public access"; principle 7, moral and material interests.

topic: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles

topic: Counter-history research piece on one lineage
claim: Cai Lun was traditionally credited with paper about 105 CE. In 1986 a fragment (2.6 × 5.6 cm) was found on the chest of the person buried in a Fangmatan tomb dated 179–141 BCE, roughly 250–280 years earlier. Yee (1994) calls it "what some believe to be a map", described as yellow paper. Reading 1: paper, drawn with a map (the excavators; Britannica's summary). Reading 2: Chen and Li (1990) argue such "paperlike objects" are not paper and the lines may be stains from the coffin's black paint; Wang Ju Hua (1990) disputes the dating.
confidence_note: Documented (the find, 1986); contested (whether paper, whether a map, the date)

topic: Counter-history research piece on one lineage

topic: Counter-history research piece on one lineage
claim: Talas, two readings. Al-Tha'alibi (d. 1038), in his *Laṭāʾif al-maʿārif*, cites the author of a *Kitāb al-masālik wa-l-mamālik*: Chinese prisoners of war "captured by Ziyad ibn Salih and brought to Samarqand" included artisans who made paper there. Ziyad commanded at Talas (751); the battle's name is the modern link. Bloom: the anecdote "is without factual basis and paper had been known—and made—in Central Asia for centuries." Hansen: "Most scholars today think" it moved west before 751.

topic: Counter-history research piece on one lineage
claim: "Papermaking was begun in Baghdad itself by the late 8th century." Its Suq al-warraqin had "more than one hundred shops for paper- and booksellers".

topic: Counter-history research piece on one lineage
claim: "The oldest dated copy of the Quran transcribed on paper" was made in 971–72, probably in Iran, by Ali ibn Shadhan al-Razi. Cleveland's two folios match the change: 1933.493 on parchment (800s), 1933.488 on paper (1100s).

topic: Counter-history research piece on one lineage
claim: The "Missal of Silos" is Santo Domingo de Silos, Biblioteca del Monasterio, MS 6. topic: Counterfactual history: a history of making that did not happen

claim: Omar ibn Said, born in Futa Toro, was "captured in 1807 and brought to South Carolina". In 1831 he wrote his life in Arabic: "I continued seeking knowledge for 25 years." The manuscript opens with Qur'anic text (Sūrat al-Mulk). LoC bought it from Sotheby's London on 30 June 2017; the collection is "free to use and reuse". The English title page reads "Owned by Governor Owen". The man who bought him, at the Fayetteville jail, was General James Owen of Bladen County, brother of Governor John Owen (Jameson, 1925; NCpedia, which dates the purchase 1810); the LoC blog's "General John Owen, the brother of the governor" reverses the brothers. He was born about 1770 and died, still enslaved, in 1863 (LoC's name record and blog) or 1864 (NCpedia; UNC).
